categories.name: Security, Identity & Compliance
categories.summary: Who can access what (IAM, Organizations, SSO), encryption and secrets, perimeter protection and threat detection.

services.name: AWS IAM
services.tagline: Global service: users, groups, roles and policies for access to AWS
facts: Global (not regional); everything is denied by default (implicit deny)
Explicit Deny always wins over Allow
Identity-based vs resource-based policies (S3 bucket policy, KMS key policy)
Roles for EC2/Lambda (instance profile) instead of access keys on the instance
Permissions boundary caps the maximum permissions of a user/role
Many users by department: IAM group + policy (e.g. read-only + aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent deny) — a role can't be attached to a group, SCPs don't apply to IAM users
Root: enable MFA, don't use it for everyday tasks
use_when: Need to give an app on EC2/Lambda access to S3/DynamoDB → IAM role
Least privilege, MFA, temporary credentials
Cross-account access → role + trust policy (AssumeRole)
Machines → IAM role (instance profile); humans (admins) → MFA + least privilege
not_for: Storing access keys in code/AMI is a trap — use a role
Authenticating users of a mobile/web app — that's Cognito
An IAM user per EC2 instance — that's just long-term keys again; use a role

vs.note: STS issues temporary credentials on AssumeRole; IAM defines roles and permissions
Identity Center — SSO for people across many accounts; IAM — within a single account
An SCP caps the maximum for an account; it grants nothing by itself

services.name: AWS STS
services.tagline: Issues temporary security credentials (AssumeRole, federation)
facts: AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, AssumeRoleWithSAML, GetSessionToken (MFA)
Credentials last from 15 min to 12 h (1 h by default)
Cross-account: role trust policy + sts:AssumeRole permission for the caller
Regional endpoints available (better latency/redundancy)

Enterprise identity federation / SSO for many corporate users to S3 or the console: no IAM user per employee. An identity provider or federation proxy (SAML 2.0, e.g. AD FS) authenticates against the corporate directory and STS issues temporary credentials for an IAM role whose IAM policy limits what the user can reach (e.g. only their own S3 folder). 3rd-party SSO products and WorkDocs are not required
use_when: Temporary access to another account
Federation with a corporate IdP (SAML)
Requirement to not store long-lived keys
not_for: Not a user directory and not an SSO portal

vs.note: IAM defines roles/policies; STS issues temporary keys based on them
Cognito Identity Pools obtain STS credentials for app users under the hood

services.name: AWS Organizations
services.tagline: Centralized management of many accounts: OUs, SCPs, consolidated billing
facts: Management account + member accounts, grouped into OUs
Modes: consolidated billing only or all features — SCPs and IAM Identity Center require all features
Consolidated billing: one bill, volume discounts, shared RI/Savings Plans pool
SCPs apply to OUs/accounts (not to the management account)
SCP = preventive guardrail for all accounts in an OU (incl. root of member accounts): e.g. deny config:DeleteConfigRule/PutConfigRule, cloudtrail:StopLogging
Tag policies, backup policies, AI opt-out policies
Organization CloudTrail trail for all accounts
use_when: Many accounts, need a single bill and discounts
Deny actions/Regions across a group of accounts at once
Create accounts automatically via API
not_for: On its own it doesn't give a landing zone with guardrails — that's Control Tower
No "external authentication" — directory sign-in is done by IAM Identity Center
Has no authentication of its own to point at Directory Service — sign-in via IAM Identity Center

vs.note: Control Tower automates a multi-account landing zone on top of Organizations
SCP is an Organizations feature for restricting permissions

services.name: Service Control Policies (SCP)
services.tagline: Guardrails in Organizations: maximum permissions for accounts/OUs
facts: They grant no permissions — they only restrict (a filter)
Apply to all users/roles in the account, including root
Don't apply to the management account or service-linked roles
Effective permissions = intersection of SCPs and IAM policies
Typical: deny outside allowed Regions, deny disabling CloudTrail
use_when: Prevent all accounts in an OU from using certain services/Regions
Even the root of a member account must not be able to do X
Centralized preventive control
not_for: Doesn't grant access — an Allow in an SCP without an IAM policy gives nothing
Doesn't affect the management account

vs.note: IAM policy grants permissions; SCP sets the upper bound
Config — detective (detect), SCP — preventive (deny)

services.name: AWS Control Tower
services.tagline: Fast multi-account landing zone with ready-made guardrails
facts: Built on Organizations, Identity Center, CloudTrail, Config
Controls (guardrails): preventive (SCP), detective (Config), proactive (CloudFormation hooks)
Account Factory — provisions new accounts per OU from preapproved baselines (incl. VPC/network config); built on Service Catalog

Per-account compliance dashboard; the easiest best-practice answer for 'set up and govern a multi-account environment with guardrails and a non-compliance dashboard' (not hand-built StackSets + Config aggregator, not Service Catalog launch constraints, not Direct Connect)
use_when: Set up a multi-account environment per best practices with LEAST operational overhead
Automatic setup of new accounts with guardrails
"Streamline creating many accounts with preapproved baselines/network configs per OU" → Control Tower (Account Factory)
not_for: Overkill for a single account

vs.note: Organizations is the base mechanism; Control Tower is ready-made automation on top
Config — rule evaluation/visibility; Control Tower — account vending + guardrails (uses Config for detective controls)

services.name: AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO)
services.tagline: SSO for employees into all Organizations accounts and business apps
facts: Formerly AWS SSO
Identity source: built-in directory, Active Directory, external IdP (Okta, Entra ID) via SAML/SCIM
Permission sets → IAM roles in target accounts
Single sign-in portal
Requires Organizations (all features); an existing on-prem AD connects via AD Connector or AWS Managed Microsoft AD (trust)
use_when: Employees must sign in once to all AWS accounts
Use corporate AD/Okta for access to AWS
not_for: Not for end users of your application — that's Cognito

vs.note: Cognito — application customers (B2C); Identity Center — employees (workforce)
Directory Service can be an identity source for Identity Center
IAM users — within one account; Identity Center — centrally across many

services.name: Amazon Cognito
services.tagline: Authentication and authorization for web/mobile app users
facts: User Pools: sign-up/sign-in, JWT tokens, MFA, social/SAML/OIDC login
Identity Pools: exchange a token for temporary AWS credentials (STS)
User Pool as an authorizer in API Gateway and ALB
Guest (unauthenticated) access supported in Identity Pools
use_when: Sign-up/sign-in for millions of mobile app users
Mobile client needs direct access to S3/DynamoDB
Login via Google/Facebook/Apple
not_for: Not for employee SSO into AWS accounts (that's Identity Center)

vs.note: Identity Center — employees; Cognito — app users
Don't create an IAM user per app user — use Cognito

services.name: AWS Directory Service
services.tagline: Managed Microsoft AD and integration with on-prem Active Directory
facts: AWS Managed Microsoft AD — full AD, trust with on-prem AD
AD Connector — proxy to on-prem AD, stores nothing in AWS
Simple AD — cheap Samba-compatible, no trust
Needed for FSx for Windows, WorkSpaces, RDS for SQL Server (Windows auth)
use_when: Apps in AWS need Active Directory / Kerberos / LDAP
Use an existing on-prem AD without replication → AD Connector
Trust between AWS and on-prem AD → Managed Microsoft AD
Sign in to AWS accounts with existing on-prem AD credentials without copying them → AD Connector + IAM Identity Center
not_for: For authenticating mobile app users — Cognito

vs.note: Identity Center can use AD as an identity source

services.name: AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)
services.tagline: Share resources between accounts without copying
facts: Shares: VPC subnets, Transit Gateway, Route 53 Resolver rules, License Manager, Aurora clusters, etc.
Within Organizations or with individual accounts
Shared VPC: participants launch resources in the owner's subnets
No additional charge
use_when: Several accounts must use one VPC/subnets
Share a Transit Gateway with all accounts in the organization
not_for: Doesn't grant IAM permissions to service APIs in general
Cannot create accounts or enforce baselines — it only shares existing resources

vs.note: Shared subnets via RAM — one VPC instead of peering many VPCs

services.name: AWS KMS
services.tagline: Managed encryption keys, integrated with almost all services
facts: AWS owned / AWS managed (aws/s3) / customer managed keys (CMK)
Symmetric (AES-256) and asymmetric; direct encryption up to 4 KB, larger — envelope encryption (data key)
Key policy is mandatory; access = key policy + IAM (e.g. Lambda: kms:Decrypt on its EXECUTION ROLE + key policy allowing that role; a Lambda resource policy only controls invocation)
Automatic CMK rotation (yearly by default, configurable)
Keys are regional; multi-Region keys for copying encrypted data
All calls logged in CloudTrail; API quotas (throttling)
use_when: Encryption at rest with key management and auditing
Need control over key rotation/policy → customer managed key
Encrypted snapshot to another account/Region
not_for: FIPS 140-2 Level 3 / single-tenant HSM with full control requirement → CloudHSM
Doesn't store passwords/secrets — that's Secrets Manager

vs.note: CloudHSM — dedicated HSM, only you manage the keys; KMS — managed multi-tenant
Secrets Manager stores secrets (and encrypts them via KMS)
ACM — TLS certificates, not data encryption keys

services.name: AWS CloudHSM
services.tagline: Dedicated hardware HSM in a VPC, keys controlled only by the customer
facts: FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated, single-tenant
AWS has no access to the keys; lose the credentials — lose the keys
HSM cluster across multiple AZs for HA
Can be attached as a custom key store for KMS
Standard APIs: PKCS#11, JCE, CNG; SSL/TLS offload
use_when: Regulatory requirement: dedicated HSM / Level 3 / full key control
Oracle TDE, SSL offload, custom crypto operations
not_for: When managed encryption with LEAST operational overhead is enough → KMS

vs.note: KMS is simpler and integrated; CloudHSM — single-tenant with full customer control

services.name: AWS Secrets Manager
services.tagline: Storage and automatic rotation of secrets (DB passwords, API keys)
facts: Automatic rotation via Lambda; built-in for RDS/Aurora/Redshift/DocumentDB
Encryption via KMS
Replication of secrets to other Regions
Paid per secret and per API call; up to 64 KB per secret
use_when: Store a DB password and rotate it automatically
Remove credentials from application code
not_for: If rotation isn't needed and cost matters — SSM Parameter Store (SecureString)

vs.note: Parameter Store is cheaper/free, but has no built-in rotation
KMS manages keys; Secrets Manager manages the secrets themselves

services.name: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)
services.tagline: Free public TLS certificates with auto-renewal
facts: Integrations: ELB, CloudFront, API Gateway (not directly on EC2)
For CloudFront (and edge-optimized API Gateway) the certificate must be in us-east-1; for ALB or a regional API Gateway endpoint it must be in that same Region
Auto-renewal for ACM-issued certificates (DNS validation)
Imported certificates are not renewed automatically
Private CA — for internal certificates (paid)
use_when: HTTPS on ALB/CloudFront with minimal maintenance
Automatic certificate renewal
not_for: A public ACM certificate cannot be exported to EC2/on-prem
Not a store for AWS access keys or secrets — it manages TLS certificates (secrets → Secrets Manager)

vs.note: KMS — data encryption keys; ACM — certificates for TLS in transit

services.name: AWS WAF
services.tagline: Web Application Firewall at L7 (HTTP)
facts: Attaches to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito User Pool
Web ACL: rules by IP, geo, headers, SQLi, XSS
Rate-based rules against HTTP floods
Managed rule groups (AWS and Marketplace)
Doesn't work on NLB (L4)
use_when: Protection against SQL injection / XSS
Block IPs/countries on ALB or CloudFront
Rate-limit requests from a single IP
not_for: Doesn't protect NLB and doesn't filter L3/L4 traffic
For L3/L4 DDoS → Shield
Not a scaling/performance tool; attaches in front of ALB/CloudFront/API Gateway/AppSync — not directly to EC2

vs.note: Shield — DDoS (L3/L4, Advanced also L7); WAF — HTTP rule filtering
Network Firewall — L3–L7 in the VPC; WAF — HTTP only, in front of the app
SG — stateful L4 allow-only; can't do SQLi/XSS

services.name: AWS Shield
services.tagline: DDoS protection: Standard is free, Advanced is extended
facts: Shield Standard — automatic and free, L3/L4
Shield Advanced: ~$3000/month per organization, 24/7 Shield Response Team
Advanced: cost protection against bill spikes caused by DDoS
Protects EC2 EIPs, ELB, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, Route 53
DDoS playbook: CloudFront + Shield/WAF + ALB with Auto Scaling + database in a private subnet; EFA (HPC bandwidth) and Dedicated Instances (isolation) do NOT mitigate DDoS
use_when: DDoS protection for a critical application
Need SRT support and cost reimbursement during an attack
not_for: Doesn't replace WAF for SQLi/XSS

vs.note: WAF — L7 rules; Shield — DDoS protection
Firewall Manager centralizes Shield Advanced and WAF across accounts

services.name: AWS Firewall Manager
services.tagline: Centralized WAF/Shield/SG/Network Firewall rules across accounts
facts: Requires Organizations and AWS Config
Automatically applies policies to new accounts and resources
Manages WAF, Shield Advanced, Security Groups, Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall
use_when: Uniform WAF rules for all accounts in the organization
New resources must get protection automatically
not_for: For a single account/resource, WAF directly is enough

vs.note: WAF — the rules themselves; Firewall Manager — rolling them out across the organization

services.name: AWS Network Firewall
services.tagline: Managed stateful firewall/IPS for VPC (L3–L7)
facts: Deployed into dedicated firewall subnets; you change VPC route tables to send traffic through the firewall endpoints (it does not attach to an ALB)
Stateful/stateless rules, Suricata-compatible IPS rules, domain filtering
Stateful domain-list rules (allow/deny FQDNs), Suricata IPS rules, managed threat lists; centralized inspection via Transit Gateway
Protects all VPC traffic (ingress/egress, VPC-to-VPC)
use_when: "Layered / defense-in-depth beyond SGs and NACLs", "block malicious URLs", "drop blacklisted FQDNs" → Network Firewall
Traffic inspection and filtering at the VPC level
Allow egress only to specific domains
IDS/IPS for a VPC
not_for: For SQLi/XSS in front of a web app, WAF is simpler

vs.note: WAF — HTTP on ALB/CloudFront; Network Firewall — all VPC traffic
NACL — stateless by IP/port per subnet; Network Firewall — deep inspection

services.name: Amazon GuardDuty
services.tagline: ML threat detection from logs (CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS)
facts: Analyzes CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs — without you enabling the logs
Protection plans: S3 Protection (suspicious S3 access via CloudTrail S3 data events), EKS, RDS login, Lambda, Runtime Monitoring, Malware Protection
Findings → EventBridge → Lambda/SNS for automated response
Detects crypto-mining, compromised credentials, communication with malicious IPs
Multi-account via delegated administrator
use_when: Continuous threat detection with LEAST operational overhead
Detect crypto-mining / suspicious API calls
"Alert on unauthorized access / suspicious access patterns / malicious activity on S3" → GuardDuty S3 Protection
not_for: Doesn't scan software vulnerabilities (that's Inspector)
Doesn't look for PII in S3 (that's Macie)

vs.note: Inspector — vulnerabilities (CVEs); GuardDuty — active threats
Macie — sensitive data in S3
Detective — root-cause investigation after GuardDuty findings

services.name: Amazon Inspector
services.tagline: Automated vulnerability scanning of EC2, ECR images, Lambda
facts: Scans for CVEs in packages and network reachability
EC2 via SSM Agent (or agentless), images in ECR, Lambda functions
Continuous scanning, risk score
Findings go to Security Hub and EventBridge
use_when: Find software vulnerabilities on EC2 / in container images
Continuous CVE assessment
not_for: Doesn't detect attacks from logs (that's GuardDuty)
Doesn't monitor S3 access — only EC2/ECR/Lambda vulnerabilities

vs.note: GuardDuty — threats from logs; Inspector — software vulnerabilities

services.name: Amazon Macie
services.tagline: ML discovery of sensitive data (PII) in S3
facts: Detects PII, financial data, credentials in S3 objects
Assesses bucket security (public, unencrypted)
Findings → EventBridge / Security Hub
S3 only
use_when: Find PII/card numbers in S3 buckets
Compliance: where sensitive data resides
not_for: Doesn't work with RDS/EBS directly

vs.note: GuardDuty — threats; Macie — data classification in S3

services.name: AWS Security Hub
services.tagline: Single pane for security findings and best-practice checks
facts: Aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Firewall Manager, partners
Standards checks: AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS, PCI DSS
Requires AWS Config
Cross-account and cross-Region aggregation
use_when: Centralized view of security posture across all accounts
Automated CIS compliance checks
not_for: Doesn't detect threats from logs itself — it aggregates
Aggregates findings; doesn't create accounts or baselines

vs.note: GuardDuty generates findings; Security Hub collects them
Config — resource configurations; Security Hub uses it for checks

services.name: Amazon Detective
services.tagline: Incident investigation: relationship graphs from logs
facts: Builds a graph from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, GuardDuty findings, EKS audit logs
Helps find the root cause
Visualizes activity over a time period
use_when: Need to investigate and find the root cause of a GuardDuty finding
After an incident, visualize which resources/IPs were involved
not_for: Doesn't detect threats on its own

vs.note: GuardDuty finds; Detective investigates

services.name: AWS Artifact
services.tagline: Portal for AWS compliance reports (SOC, PCI, ISO) and agreements
facts: Download SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, ISO reports
Accept agreements (BAA for HIPAA)
Self-service, no additional charge
use_when: Auditor needs an AWS compliance report (SOC/PCI)
Sign a BAA
not_for: Doesn't check your resources for compliance (that's Audit Manager/Config)

vs.note: Audit Manager collects evidence about your resources; Artifact — reports about AWS

services.name: AWS Audit Manager
services.tagline: Continuous audit evidence collection for your AWS resources
facts: Prebuilt frameworks: GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2
Automatically collects evidence from Config, CloudTrail, Security Hub
Generates reports for auditors
use_when: Automate audit preparation
Collect evidence of control compliance
not_for: Doesn't provide compliance reports about AWS itself (that's Artifact)

vs.note: Artifact — AWS reports; Audit Manager — evidence about your environment
Config — rule evaluation; Audit Manager uses it as an evidence source

categories.name: Networking & Content Delivery
categories.summary: VPC and its components, hybrid connectivity with on-prem, load balancing, DNS and global content delivery.

services.name: Amazon VPC
services.tagline: Isolated virtual network in a Region
facts: Regional; spans all AZs of the Region, subnets live in a single AZ
CIDR from /16 to /28; secondary CIDRs can be added
Default VPC in every Region (public subnets)
IPv6 dual-stack supported; up to 5 VPCs per Region (soft limit)
Route tables, IGW, NAT, endpoints, SG, NACL — the building blocks

DNS attributes: DNS resolution (enableDnsSupport) + DNS hostnames (enableDnsHostnames); both must be on for instance DNS hostnames and for private hosted zones; a VPC from the wizard/default VPC has them on, one created via CLI/API has hostnames off; Route 53, CIDR and SGs are not the cause
use_when: Isolate resources in your own network
Separate public/private tiers
not_for: VPCs with overlapping CIDRs can't be peered

vs.note: Peering connects two VPCs; the VPC is the network itself
TGW — hub for many VPCs and on-prem

services.name: Subnets & Route Tables
services.tagline: IP range in one AZ; public or private depending on the route table
facts: Subnet = one AZ
AWS reserves 5 IPs in every subnet (first 4 and the last)
Every route table has an implicit local route (VPC CIDR → local): all subnets in a VPC reach each other without IGW/NAT
Public = route 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW; private — without it
For HA — subnets in at least 2 AZs
use_when: Split tiers: ALB in public, app and DB in private
Multi-AZ deployment
not_for: A /28 subnet gives only 11 usable IPs — a calculation trap
Intra-VPC connectivity problems are never fixed by NAT/IGW routes — check SGs and NACLs

vs.note: NACL applies at the subnet level

services.name: Security Groups
services.tagline: Stateful firewall at the ENI/instance level, allow only
facts: Stateful: return traffic is allowed automatically
Allow rules only, no deny

Source can be another SG (SG reference): DB rule (e.g. TCP 1433/3306) with Source = the app tier's SG ID is the least-privilege answer and survives Auto Scaling; not instance IDs, NACL IDs or static IPs
Default: all inbound denied, all outbound allowed
All rules are evaluated
use_when: Allow the DB to accept traffic only from the app's SG
Access control at the instance level
Bastion pattern: bastion SG allows SSH/RDP only from corporate IPs; instance SGs allow it only from the bastion SG
not_for: Can't block a specific IP (no deny) → NACL or WAF

vs.note: NACL — stateless, subnet-level, has deny and rule ordering
WAF — L7 rules for HTTP

services.name: Network ACLs
services.tagline: Stateless firewall at the subnet level, allow and deny
facts: Stateless: return traffic must be explicitly allowed (ephemeral ports 1024–65535)
Open HTTPS to the world = SG inbound 443 + NACL inbound 443 AND NACL outbound ephemeral (e.g. 32768-65535) — outbound 443 is wrong
Rules by number, first match wins
Has deny — can block specific IPs
Default NACL allows everything; a custom one denies everything by default
use_when: Block a specific IP/range at the subnet level
Additional layer of subnet protection
Two subnets in one VPC can't talk → check NACLs of both subnets (+ SGs)
not_for: Forgetting ephemeral ports in outbound is a common cause of broken connectivity

vs.note: SG — stateful, instance, allow only; NACL — stateless, subnet, allow+deny
Network Firewall — deep inspection; NACL — simple IP/port rules

services.name: Internet Gateway
services.tagline: Internet Gateway: VPC access to the internet (both directions)
facts: One IGW per VPC, horizontally scaled, HA
Instance needs a public IP/Elastic IP + route 0.0.0.0/0 → IGW
Egress-only IGW — outbound IPv6 with no inbound
use_when: Make a subnet public
Instances must be reachable from the internet
not_for: A private subnet must not have a route to the IGW — use NAT for outbound

vs.note: NAT — outbound-only IPv4 from a private subnet; IGW — bidirectional

services.name: NAT Gateway
services.tagline: Managed NAT: outbound internet for private subnets
facts: Placed in a public subnet, needs an Elastic IP (public NAT)
Zonal: for HA — one NAT Gateway per AZ
Up to 100 Gbps, managed; NAT instance — legacy self-managed alternative
Charged per hour + per GB processed — expensive with heavy traffic to S3
Doesn't support SGs
use_when: Private instances need updates from the internet without inbound access
Replace a NAT instance with LEAST operational overhead
not_for: Traffic to S3/DynamoDB through NAT is expensive — use a Gateway endpoint
One NAT for all AZs — single point of failure
Doesn't filter domains/URLs — it only gives private subnets outbound internet

vs.note: IGW — bidirectional access for public; NAT — outbound only
Gateway endpoint to S3/DynamoDB is free and needs no NAT

services.name: Bastion Host (jump box)
services.tagline: Hardened EC2 in a public subnet used as the only admin entry point
facts: Lives in a public subnet with a public/Elastic IP
Bastion SG: SSH 22 (Linux) / RDP 3389 (Windows) only from corporate public IP ranges
SSH/RDP are TCP (never UDP); a single IP is written as x.x.x.x/32 — /0 means the whole internet
Instance SGs: allow SSH/RDP only from the bastion's SG (SG reference)
Make it HA with an Auto Scaling group across AZs
Modern alternative: SSM Session Manager — no bastion, no open ports, audited
use_when: "Limit administrative access to instances in private subnets over the Internet"
Company has no VPN/DX to the VPC and needs RDP/SSH admin access
not_for: Private subnet bastion — unreachable from the Internet even with an EIP
Opening SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0
LEAST operational overhead / no open ports → Session Manager

vs.note: Session Manager replaces bastions: no inbound ports, IAM-controlled, logged
SG reference: instances trust only the bastion's SG

services.name: VPC Endpoints (Gateway / Interface)
services.tagline: Private access to AWS services without IGW/NAT
facts: Gateway endpoint: S3 and DynamoDB, added as a target in route tables (prefix list), free — the default exam answer for private S3/DynamoDB access

Gateway endpoint for DynamoDB (also from EKS/Fargate pods in private subnets): you create it and associate it with the route tables of the subnets — a NACL rule cannot route to it, Network Firewall rules do not replace it, and a DynamoDB interface endpoint is not what the exam expects (DAX/DynamoDB calls stay on the AWS network via the gateway endpoint)
Interface endpoint (PrivateLink): ENI with a private IP, most services, paid

Cheapest fix for "private-subnet EC2 must reach S3 without the internet" = S3 Gateway endpoint (free, route table). Interface endpoint for S3 costs per hour + per GB and is only needed from on-premises / another Region / other VPCs; a VPN or a custom endpoint service (your own service behind an NLB) is not the way to reach S3. Pre-signed URLs given to internet users are served by S3 directly and are unaffected by how the app reaches S3
Interface endpoint is reachable from on-prem via VPN/DX; Gateway is not
Endpoint policy = what can be reached THROUGH the endpoint (e.g. only trusted bucket ARNs); bucket policy with aws:SourceVpce/aws:SourceVpc = who may reach the bucket
use_when: Private subnet → S3 without internet and at minimal cost → Gateway endpoint
Access to SQS/KMS/SSM from a private subnet without NAT → Interface endpoint
Allow a bucket only from a specific VPC endpoint
"VPC may reach only trusted buckets via the gateway endpoint" → endpoint policy listing those buckets
not_for: Gateway endpoint doesn't work from on-prem or from a peered VPC
Interface endpoints are ENIs in subnets (private DNS) — they are not "associated with route tables"; NACLs filter CIDRs, not endpoint DNS names

vs.note: NAT is charged per GB; Gateway endpoint for S3 is free
Interface endpoint is built on PrivateLink

services.name: AWS PrivateLink
services.tagline: Private access to a service in another VPC/account via ENI
facts: Provider: NLB (or GWLB) + endpoint service; consumer: interface endpoint
One-way access to a specific service, not the whole VPC
Works with overlapping CIDRs
Scales to thousands of consumers (SaaS)
use_when: Expose a service to hundreds of customer VPCs without peering
CIDRs overlap, peering impossible
Access to only one application, not the whole network
not_for: Not for full connectivity between VPCs (that's peering/TGW)

vs.note: Peering — whole network, no CIDR overlap; PrivateLink — one service, overlap OK
TGW — transitive routing across many networks

services.name: VPC Peering
services.tagline: Direct connection of two VPCs (incl. cross-account/Region)
facts: Non-transitive: A↔B and B↔C don't give A↔C
DEV↔UAT + UAT↔PROD ≠ DEV↔PROD: create a direct DEV↔PROD peering + routes both ways
CIDRs must not overlap
Routes needed in route tables on both sides
No charge for the connection; inter-AZ/Region traffic is paid
No edge-to-edge routing (via the peer's IGW/VPN)
use_when: Connect a few VPCs cheaply and simply
Cross-account access between two VPCs
not_for: Many VPCs (full mesh) → Transit Gateway
Overlapping CIDRs → PrivateLink
On-prem reaching VPC-A through VPC-B's VPN/DX/IGW — impossible (no edge-to-edge routing)

vs.note: TGW — hub-and-spoke, transitive, for tens/hundreds of VPCs
PrivateLink — access to one service, allows CIDR overlap

services.name: AWS Transit Gateway
services.tagline: Regional hub connecting thousands of VPCs and on-prem (transitively)
facts: Hub-and-spoke, transitive routing
Attaches VPCs, VPN, Direct Connect (via DX Gateway)
Inter-Region peering between TGWs; sharing via RAM
TGW route tables for segmentation
ECMP across multiple VPN tunnels to increase throughput

Hundreds of VPCs + VPNs across Regions in one fabric: one TGW per Region, TGW peering attachments between Regions (static routes), shared across accounts with RAM; peering, DX gateway or VPN CloudHub alone cannot do this
use_when: Many VPCs + on-prem, simplify a complex peering mesh
Increase VPN throughput (ECMP)
not_for: For 2–3 VPCs, peering is cheaper

vs.note: Peering — point-to-point, non-transitive; TGW — central hub
DX attaches to TGW via Direct Connect Gateway (transit VIF)

services.name: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
services.tagline: IPsec VPN between on-prem and AWS over the internet
facts: VGW or TGW on the AWS side; on-prem: Customer Gateway device with a static, Internet-routable public IP (behind NAT only with NAT-T)
2 tunnels for redundancy; ~1.25 Gbps per tunnel
Set up in minutes, cheaper than Direct Connect
IPsec encryption; can be a backup for DX
VPN CloudHub — connecting multiple offices via VGW
VPC side: route to the VGW (or enable route propagation); VGW tunnel endpoints are AWS-managed — no Elastic IP to attach
use_when: Connect on-prem quickly (days/hours)
Encrypted backup link for Direct Connect
Encryption over Direct Connect
not_for: Need consistent latency/high throughput → Direct Connect
VPN CloudHub does not create Direct Connect connections — it's hub-and-spoke VPN between branch sites
NAT instance/Gateway or an EIP on the VGW are never VPN requirements

vs.note: DX — dedicated link, consistent, but slow to set up (weeks) and unencrypted by default
Client VPN — for individual users, not for a network

services.name: AWS Client VPN
services.tagline: Managed OpenVPN user access to VPC/on-prem
facts: Clients use OpenVPN-compatible software
Authentication: AD, SAML, certificates (mutual TLS)
Associated with VPC subnets
use_when: Remote employees must connect securely to private resources
Employee access to on-prem via a VPC connected over VPN/DX
not_for: Not for connecting office networks (that's Site-to-Site VPN)

vs.note: S2S — network to network; Client VPN — user's laptop to VPC

services.name: AWS Direct Connect
services.tagline: Dedicated private link from on-prem to AWS
facts: Dedicated 1/10/100 Gbps or Hosted from 50 Mbps to 25 Gbps via a partner
Provisioning takes weeks
Not encrypted by default → VPN over DX or MACsec
VIF: private (VPC), public (AWS public services), transit (TGW)
Direct Connect Gateway — access to VPCs in different Regions and accounts; associates only with a virtual private gateway or a Transit Gateway (transit VIF), NOT with VPC peering
New accounts sharing an existing DX: DX Gateway + Transit Gateway (no new DX per account)
HA: two DX connections in different locations; cheap option — DX + VPN backup
use_when: Consistent latency and high throughput
Large recurring data volumes, reduce egress cost
Private connection without the internet
not_for: Need to connect urgently — DX takes long; use VPN temporarily
Encryption is not enabled by default
A DX/VPN into a peered VPC gives no resiliency for the other VPC — the backup must terminate on the same VPC (or use TGW / DX Gateway)

vs.note: VPN — fast and encrypted over the internet; DX — consistent, dedicated, slow to provision
Transit VIF + DX Gateway connect DX to TGW

services.name: VPC Flow Logs
services.tagline: IP traffic metadata logs for VPC/subnet/ENI
facts: Delivered to CloudWatch Logs, S3 or Firehose
Metadata (src/dst IP, port, ACCEPT/REJECT), not packet contents
Levels: VPC, subnet, ENI
Analysis via Athena or CloudWatch Logs Insights
use_when: Troubleshooting: why traffic is blocked (SG/NACL)
Auditing network connections
not_for: Don't capture payload — that's Traffic Mirroring

vs.note: CloudTrail — API calls; Flow Logs — network traffic
GuardDuty analyzes flow logs automatically

services.name: Elastic Load Balancing (ALB / NLB / GWLB)
services.tagline: Load balancers: ALB (L7), NLB (L4), GWLB (L3)
facts: ALB: HTTP/HTTPS, path/host/header routing, targets EC2/IP/Lambda, WAF, auth via Cognito
NLB: TCP/UDP/TLS, millions of rps, ultra-low latency, static IP / Elastic IP per AZ
GWLB: proxy for third-party appliances (firewall, IDS), GENEVE 6081
Health checks; cross-zone balancing (on by default for ALB)
Sticky sessions, SSL termination via ACM, SNI
Many domains on one ALB HTTPS listener: attach multiple certificates (default + additional), ALB picks by SNI — free; wildcard = one domain's subdomains only, SAN needs reissue
Connection draining (deregistration delay)

HTTP→HTTPS redirect: edit the EXISTING port-80 listener (default action or host-header rule) with a redirect action to HTTPS:443 (301); one listener per port, so no second :80 listener; the 443 listener never sees HTTP traffic
use_when: Routing by URL path/hostname, microservices → ALB
Clients must whitelist the endpoint's IPs on their firewall → NLB with an Elastic IP per AZ
Need static IP, TCP/UDP, extreme performance → NLB
Route traffic through a third-party firewall → GWLB
not_for: WAF can't be attached to NLB
ALB doesn't provide a static IP (put an NLB in front of ALB, or Global Accelerator)
Elastic IP on an ALB — impossible; ALB IPs change as it scales
ALB host-based routing forwards by Host header — it's not threat filtering
Swapping ALB for NLB doesn't fix a database bottleneck

vs.note: GA — global anycast IPs and cross-Region routing; ELB — within one Region
API Gateway — API management (throttling, keys); ALB — simple load balancing
Route 53 — DNS-level balancing across Regions

services.name: Amazon Route 53
services.tagline: Managed DNS, domain registration and routing policies
facts: Routing: simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity, multivalue, IP-based
Geolocation = WHERE the user is (country/continent → fixed endpoint, all-or-nothing); Geoproximity = HOW FAR (nearest resource, bias −99..+99 grows/shrinks a Region's area — "shift a larger portion")
Alias record — free, works at the zone apex, points to AWS resources (ELB, CloudFront, S3)
CNAME not allowed at the zone apex
Failover routing: primary record + health check, secondary → DR; Evaluate Target Health (alias to ELB) inherits target health; health checkers must be allowed by NACL/SG
Private hosted zones for VPC; Resolver endpoints for hybrid DNS
100% availability SLA
use_when: Active-passive failover between Regions
Route users to the lowest-latency Region
Content by user's country (geolocation)
Blue/green, canary via weighted
"Route a larger portion of traffic from area X to Region Y" → geoproximity with positive bias
Spread traffic across multiple instances/endpoints at DNS level → weighted (or multivalue answer) with health checks
not_for: DNS failover depends on TTL and client caching — not instant (GA is faster)
Geolocation can't send a 'larger portion' — it maps whole locations; proportional shift = geoproximity bias, % split for everyone = weighted
Weighted routing for "DR only on outage" — weighted always splits traffic; custom Lambda calling ChangeResourceRecordSets — reinvents failover routing

vs.note: GA — anycast IPs, failover in seconds without DNS caching
ELB — within a Region; Route 53 — across Regions
CloudFront caches content; Route 53 only resolves names

services.name: Amazon CloudFront
services.tagline: Global CDN: caching at edge locations
facts: Origins: S3, ALB, EC2, any HTTP; Origin Access Control (OAC) for private S3

Signed URLs / signed cookies for private content — private content for specific clients = signed URLs/cookies (who) + OAC on the S3 origin (only via CloudFront); Origin Shield is caching not security; S3 presigned URL bypasses CloudFront
Geo restriction, WAF, Shield; HTTPS with an ACM certificate from us-east-1
Cache behaviors by path, TTL, invalidation
Lambda@Edge (viewer/origin request+response, can rewrite URI by User-Agent, full Node/Python) vs CloudFront Functions (viewer events only, ultra-light header/URL logic)
Origin failover via origin groups
Response headers policy: add/override response headers (security, CORS, custom) — cannot choose content by request

Global real-time clickstream/user-activity processing close to users with low latency = CloudFront + Lambda@Edge (compute at the edge) + Kinesis (streaming) + S3 (durable results); Route 53 latency/geoproximity routing only steers DNS and processes nothing; Athena is interactive SQL over S3, not a stream processor
use_when: Reduce latency for static/dynamic content worldwide
Serve private S3 content only via the CDN (OAC)
Reduce load on the origin
"Static content to users worldwide, reduce server costs, secure" → S3 origin + CloudFront (no servers at all)
Many clients worldwide repeatedly download the same S3 objects (updates, media) → CloudFront caching; CachingDisabled defeats the purpose
Serve different variants (WebP/JPEG, mobile/desktop) by User-Agent/Accept + add headers → Lambda@Edge
not_for: Not for non-HTTP protocols (TCP/UDP games) → Global Accelerator
Custom origin on private IPs of web servers — origin must be publicly reachable; CloudFront edge IPs aren't a fixed whitelistable set
Route 53 can't route by HTTP headers (User-Agent) — that's CloudFront/Lambda@Edge logic

vs.note: GA — TCP/UDP, no caching, static anycast IPs; CloudFront — HTTP cache
S3 Transfer Acceleration — faster uploads to S3; CloudFront — content delivery

services.name: AWS Global Accelerator
services.tagline: Anycast static IPs and routing over the AWS network to the nearest Region
facts: 2 static anycast IPs per application
Endpoints: ALB, NLB, EC2, Elastic IP in one or many Regions
Health checks, failover in < 1 minute, no DNS caching
TCP and UDP, no caching
Traffic dials and endpoint weights
use_when: Non-HTTP workloads: gaming (UDP), IoT (MQTT), VoIP
Need fixed IPs for customer whitelisting
Fast regional failover without DNS TTL
HTTP only when it specifically needs static IPs or deterministic, fast regional failover
not_for: Need content caching → CloudFront
Static files / S3 — GA can't use S3 as an endpoint and doesn't cache

vs.note: CloudFront — HTTP cache at the edge; GA — TCP/UDP proxy with static IPs, no cache
Route 53 failover depends on DNS TTL; GA switches faster

services.name: Amazon API Gateway
services.tagline: Managed front door for REST/HTTP/WebSocket APIs
facts: REST API (full feature set: API keys, usage plans, caching, request validation) and HTTP API (cheaper, simpler)
WebSocket API for two-way communication
Integration timeout 29 s by default
Throttling, usage plans, API keys, response caching
Auth: IAM, Cognito User Pools, Lambda authorizer
Endpoint types: edge-optimized, regional, private

Custom domain (api.example.com) + HTTPS: ACM certificate in the SAME Region as a regional API (us-east-1 only for edge-optimized), custom domain name + base path mapping to the stage, Route 53 alias record to the API Gateway domain name (not a CNAME to the invoke URL)
use_when: Serverless API: API Gateway + Lambda
Rate limiting / API keys for clients
Real-time chat via WebSocket
not_for: Long requests > 29 s are a trap (use async)

vs.note: ALB is cheaper for sustained high traffic, but has no usage plans/API keys
API Gateway — HTTP front end; Lambda — the logic (also Function URL)

categories.name: Compute
categories.summary: EC2 virtual machines, pricing models, scaling, and PaaS/hybrid compute options.

services.name: Amazon EC2
services.tagline: Virtual servers (instances) with full OS control
facts: Families: general (M, T), compute (C), memory (R, X), storage (I, D), accelerated (P, G, Inf)
T instances are burstable (CPU credits)
User data — script at first boot; instance metadata 169.254.169.254 (IMDSv2)
Role via instance profile, not access keys
Stop/start changes the host and public IP (except Elastic IP); hibernate saves RAM to EBS
ENI: secondary ENIs keep private IP/MAC/SGs and can be moved to another instance in the same AZ (failover); the primary ENI (eth0) can't be detached
use_when: Need full control of OS/software, legacy applications
Long-running workloads, specific hardware (GPU)
"Keep the same private IP and fail over to another instance" → move a secondary ENI
not_for: If LEAST operational overhead is required — Lambda/Fargate/Beanstalk are often better
Elastic IP for a private-IP endpoint — EIPs are public addresses

vs.note: Lambda — serverless, up to 15 min; EC2 — full control and any duration
Fargate — containers without managing instances

services.name: EC2 Purchasing Options (On-Demand / RI / Savings Plans / Spot)
services.tagline: EC2 pricing models: On-Demand, RI, Savings Plans, Spot, Dedicated
facts: On-Demand — no commitment, for short unpredictable workloads
Reserved Instances / Savings Plans — 1 or 3 years, up to ~72% discount
Compute Savings Plans are more flexible (any family/Region, Fargate, Lambda); EC2 Instance SP — family+Region

Spot — up to 90% discount, can be interrupted with a 2-min notice; no bid price since 2018, you only set an optional max price. Best for queue-driven, interruption-tolerant extra capacity (video transcoding backlog polling SQS: an interrupted job is re-processed by another instance) that is only needed until the backlog is gone
Dedicated Hosts — socket/core-level BYOL, compliance; Dedicated Instances — hardware isolation

Capacity Reservations — guaranteed capacity in a specific AZ for any duration (no 1/3-year term, cancel any time, billed from the moment active even if unused); no discount by itself but Savings Plans / Regional RIs apply to it. A Regional RI gives the discount but does NOT reserve capacity; only a Zonal RI does (1-3 year term). Nightly batch that must not be delayed or interrupted and only runs a few hours = Capacity Reservation (create/cancel by automation), not Dedicated Hosts (BYOL, idle the rest of the day)

Launch limits: On-Demand instances are limited by vCPU-based quotas per Region (not per AZ and not a flat 20 instances); new accounts start lower; when requests start failing after N successes, request a quota increase (Service Quotas / limit form) for that Region and retry; there is also a 20 Standard Reserved Instances per Region limit and a dynamic Spot limit
Billing by state: running = billed; pending / stopped / Spot-stopping = not billed; stopping-to-hibernate = billed; Reserved Instances bill for the whole term even if terminated

Billing by state: stopping-to-hibernate IS billed, stopping-to-stop, pending and Spot stopping are not; Reserved Instances on terminated instances are billed to the end of the term (sell Standard RIs on the RI Marketplace; snapshot EBS then terminate)
use_when: Steady 24/7 workload for years → RI / Savings Plans
Interruptible batch/CI jobs, stateless → Spot
Per-socket/per-core licenses (BYOL) → Dedicated Hosts
Guarantee capacity for an event → Capacity Reservation
not_for: Spot for a critical DB or a workload that can't be interrupted — a trap
RI for a short-term project — overpaying
Unneeded Reserved Instances: stopping doesn't stop the charge — terminate the instances and sell Standard RIs on the Reserved Instance Marketplace (Convertible RIs can't be sold)

vs.note: ASG with a mixed instances policy combines On-Demand and Spot
Cost Explorer gives RI/Savings Plans recommendations

services.name: EC2 Placement Groups
services.tagline: Instance placement strategies: cluster, spread, partition
facts: Cluster — one AZ, low latency and 10–100 Gbps between instances (HPC)
Spread — each instance on separate hardware, max 7 instances per AZ
Partition — groups of racks, up to 7 partitions per AZ, for Hadoop/Cassandra/Kafka
Free

EFA (Elastic Fabric Adapter) = ENA + OS-bypass: a NIC for HPC/ML inter-node traffic with lower latency and higher throughput than TCP (SRD protocol; MPI/NCCL libraries; Linux only; use with a cluster placement group) — a performance feature, not a security one

ENA = enhanced networking (up to 100 Gbps, no OS-bypass); plain ENI = just a virtual network card (private IP, SG, MAC) with no HPC acceleration; a private VIF is a Direct Connect concept, not attachable to EC2
use_when: HPC, low latency between nodes → cluster
Maximum isolation of a small number of critical instances → spread
Large distributed rack-aware systems → partition
not_for: Cluster gives no HA — everything in one AZ/rack

vs.note: A placement group affects only the physical placement of EC2

services.name: EC2 Auto Scaling
services.tagline: Auto Scaling Group: automatic EC2 count based on load and health
facts: Min/desired/max; launch template (holds the AMI — new AMI = new launch template or version, then instance refresh for existing instances; target group is unrelated)
Policies: target tracking (simplest), step, simple, scheduled, predictive
EC2 or ELB health checks; replaces unhealthy instances
Spread across multiple AZs; cooldown/warm-up
Mixed instances (On-Demand + Spot); warm pools; lifecycle hooks
Default termination policy: balance AZs, then oldest launch template

Avoid over-provisioning without hurting performance = target tracking scaling (keeps a metric at a target, scales in and out); simple scaling waits for cooldown, scheduled is for predictable patterns, suspend/resume is not a policy
use_when: Keep CPU at ~50% → target tracking
Known peak on a schedule → scheduled scaling
Self-healing when an instance fails
Predictable load cycles → predictive scaling
not_for: Doesn't scale RDS — for reads use read replicas / Aurora Auto Scaling

vs.note: ELB distributes traffic; ASG changes the number of instances
Mixed instances policy reduces cost via Spot

services.name: Amazon Machine Image (AMI)
services.tagline: Image for launching EC2 (OS + software + configuration)
facts: Regional; copied to other Regions (copy AMI)
Can be shared with other accounts or made public
Golden AMI speeds up launch (less user data)
EC2 Image Builder automates building and patching
Encrypted AMI: sharing requires sharing the KMS key
use_when: Fast launch of instances with preconfigured software
DR in another Region — copy the AMI
not_for: An AMI from another Region can't be used without copying

vs.note: AMI — template, EC2 — running instance

services.name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
services.tagline: PaaS: upload code — AWS deploys EC2, ELB, ASG
facts: Supports Java, .NET, Node.js, Python, PHP, Ruby, Go, Docker
Pay only for the underlying resources
Deployment: all at once, rolling, rolling with batch, immutable, traffic splitting, blue/green (swap URL)
Web server and worker environments (worker reads from SQS)
use_when: Quickly deploy a web app for developers without infrastructure knowledge
LEAST operational overhead for a classic web app on EC2
not_for: Full infrastructure control/IaC for many services → CloudFormation

vs.note: CloudFormation — IaC for any resources; Beanstalk — ready-made application platform
App Runner — even simpler, from a container/code without EC2

services.name: AWS Batch
services.tagline: Managed batch jobs on EC2/Spot/Fargate
facts: Job queues, job definitions (Docker), compute environments
Automatically selects and scales capacity
No 15-min limit like Lambda
Spot support for savings, array jobs, multi-node parallel
use_when: Thousands of compute jobs, long-running > 15 min
Batch processing with automatic provisioning
not_for: Short event-driven processing → Lambda
Simple file-format ETL (CSV→Parquet) → Glue; Batch means your own containers/code

vs.note: Lambda — up to 15 min, event-driven; Batch — long-running jobs in containers
Step Functions can orchestrate Batch jobs

services.name: AWS Outposts
services.tagline: AWS infrastructure (racks/servers) in your data center
facts: Same APIs; EC2, EBS, ECS, EKS, RDS, S3 on Outposts locally
AWS installs and maintains it; you're responsible for physical security
Connects to a parent Region
use_when: Low latency to on-prem systems, data must stay local (data residency)
Consistent AWS experience in a hybrid environment
not_for: If you just need to migrate to the cloud — that's not Outposts

Outposts runs EC2 at your site

services.name: Amazon Lightsail
services.tagline: Simple fixed-price VPS for small projects
facts: Bundle: instance, SSD, data transfer, DNS, static IP
Ready-made images (WordPress, LAMP), managed DB, load balancer
Limited integration with the rest of AWS

Need to spin up a server quickly with minimal cloud knowledge
not_for: Not for scalable enterprise architectures

categories.name: Serverless & Containers
categories.summary: Compute without managing servers: functions, containers, orchestration and workflows.

services.name: AWS Lambda
services.tagline: Event-driven serverless functions, pay per execution time
facts: Max timeout 15 min; memory 128 MB – 10 GB (CPU scales proportionally)
Ephemeral /tmp up to 10 GB; deployment package 50 MB zip / 250 MB unzipped, container image up to 10 GB
Default concurrency 1000 per Region (soft); reserved and provisioned concurrency
Provisioned concurrency / SnapStart — against cold starts
Triggers: S3, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis, API Gateway, ALB

use_when: Event-driven processing (upload to S3 → process)
Irregular load, pay only for usage
LEAST operational overhead for short tasks
Consume Kinesis/SQS/DynamoDB Streams via event source mapping — serverless async processing
not_for: Tasks longer than 15 min → Fargate/Batch/EC2
Sustained high load can be more expensive than containers
Orchestrating an EMR cluster from Lambda for simple ETL — more moving parts than Glue

Step Functions orchestrates multiple Lambdas and long workflows

services.name: Amazon ECS
services.tagline: AWS container orchestrator (EC2 or Fargate launch type)
facts: Task definition, task, service, cluster
Launch types: EC2 (you manage instances) or Fargate (serverless)
Task role (IAM for the container) vs execution role (pull from ECR, logs)
Integration with ALB (dynamic port mapping), Service Auto Scaling
Capacity providers, Fargate Spot

Microservices behind an ALB
not_for: If Kubernetes API/portability is required → EKS

services.name: Amazon EKS
services.tagline: Managed Kubernetes control plane
facts: Worker nodes: managed node groups, self-managed, Fargate, Auto Mode
Compatible with upstream Kubernetes
IRSA / EKS Pod Identity for pod-level IAM
Can run on-prem (EKS Anywhere) and on Outposts

Already using Kubernetes, migrating k8s workloads
Need portability across clouds/on-prem
not_for: If Kubernetes isn't required — ECS is simpler

services.name: AWS Fargate
services.tagline: Serverless compute for ECS/EKS containers
facts: No EC2 instances to manage
You set vCPU and memory per task/pod; pay for task resources
Fargate Spot — up to 70% cheaper, interruptible

Tasks longer than 15 min, but without managing servers
not_for: Need GPU or host access → ECS/EKS on EC2

ECS on EC2 — cheaper at high utilization, but you manage instances

services.name: Amazon ECR
services.tagline: Private/public Docker registry
facts: Stores images in S3 under the hood, encryption, IAM access
Image scanning (basic, and enhanced via Inspector)
Lifecycle policies to delete old images
Cross-Region and cross-account replication
use_when: Store container images for ECS/EKS/Lambda
Scan images for vulnerabilities

services.name: AWS App Runner
services.tagline: Fully managed running of web apps from code or a container
facts: Build, deploy, load balancing, TLS, autoscaling — automatic
Source: ECR image or a code repository
VPC connector for access to private resources

Containerized API with autoscaling and LEAST operational overhead
not_for: Need fine-grained networking/orchestration control → ECS/EKS
Not an open-source orchestration platform — proprietary, fully managed web/API runner

services.name: AWS Step Functions

facts: Standard: up to 1 year, exactly-once; Express: up to 5 min, high rate, at-least-once
Built-in retry, catch, parallel, map, wait, choice
Direct integrations with 200+ services (SDK integrations)
Human approval via callback (task token)

Long-running process waiting for human approval

categories.name: Storage
categories.summary: Object (S3/Glacier), block (EBS, instance store) and file (EFS, FSx) storage, hybrid and backup.

services.name: Amazon S3
services.tagline: Object storage: unlimited capacity, 11 nines of durability
facts: Objects up to 5 TB; multipart upload recommended > 100 MB, required > 5 GB
Strong read-after-write consistency for all operations
Durability 99.999999999%; bucket names are globally unique, the bucket is regional
Versioning, Object Lock (WORM), event notifications (Lambda/SQS/SNS/EventBridge)
Static website hosting; presigned URLs for temporary access

Transfer Acceleration — faster, more consistent uploads from distant/global users via the nearest edge location + AWS backbone (accelerate endpoint; pair with multipart); not for downloads caching → CloudFront; not Direct Connect/FTP/OAC
use_when: Store unstructured data, backups, data lakes
Static website / media for CloudFront
Temporary access to an object without AWS credentials → presigned URL
Purely static website (HTML/CSS/JS/images) → S3 website hosting + CloudFront, no servers
not_for: Not a file system with POSIX locking (that's EFS/FSx)
Not for low-latency OS block storage (that's EBS)

EBS — block disk for a single instance
CloudFront caches S3 content worldwide

services.name: S3 Storage Classes
services.tagline: S3 classes by access frequency and cost
facts: Standard; Intelligent-Tiering — automatic movement for unknown patterns, no retrieval fee
Standard-IA and One Zone-IA: min 30 days, retrieval fee; One Zone — single AZ
Glacier Instant Retrieval (ms, min 90 days), Flexible Retrieval (minutes–hours, min 90 days), Deep Archive (up to 12–48 h, min 180 days)
Express One Zone — single-digit ms latency, single AZ, directory buckets
All have 11 nines of durability (One Zone loses data if the AZ is lost)
use_when: Unknown/changing access pattern → Intelligent-Tiering
Infrequent access, but instant → Standard-IA / Glacier Instant Retrieval
Reproducible data, infrequent → One Zone-IA
Archive for years, cheapest → Deep Archive
not_for: One Zone-IA for irreplaceable data — a trap
IA for objects < 128 KB or short-lived — overpaying
One Zone-IA when the stem says "highly available" — single AZ

vs.note: Lifecycle moves objects between classes by age
Glacier classes — archival storage

services.name: S3 Lifecycle Policies
services.tagline: Rules for automatic transition and deletion of objects
facts: Transition actions (to IA/Glacier) and expiration actions
Filter by prefix/tag; actions for noncurrent versions
Delete incomplete multipart uploads
Minimum 30 days in Standard before transitioning to IA
use_when: After 30 days to IA, after 90 to Glacier, delete after 7 years
Reduce cost with a known access pattern
not_for: Pattern unknown — Intelligent-Tiering is better
If data is cold from day one, upload directly to the cold class — landing in Standard then transitioning adds cost

vs.note: Lifecycle moves objects between classes

services.name: S3 Replication (CRR / SRR)
services.tagline: Asynchronous object replication between buckets (CRR/SRR)
facts: CRR — to another Region; SRR — within the same Region; S3 is already multi-AZ, so a Region failure (not an AZ outage) = Cross-Region Replication, not lifecycle to Glacier, EC2 copies or cross-account access
Requires versioning on both buckets
Only new objects are replicated; for existing ones — S3 Batch Replication
Replication Time Control (RTC): 99.99% within 15 minutes
Delete markers optional; can change owner and storage class
use_when: DR / compliance copy in another Region → CRR
Reduce latency for users in another Region
Aggregate logs from several buckets → SRR
not_for: Existing objects are not replicated automatically

vs.note: AWS Backup — point-in-time backups; replication — live copy

services.name: S3 Security (Bucket Policy, Block Public Access, Object Lock, Encryption)
services.tagline: S3 access and encryption: policies, Block Public Access, SSE
facts: Default encryption SSE-S3 (AES-256, keys managed AND rotated automatically by AWS — least overhead); also SSE-KMS, DSSE-KMS, SSE-C, client-side; to forbid unencrypted uploads: bucket policy denying s3:PutObject unless x-amz-server-side-encryption is AES256 (or aws:kms) — an SCP cannot target a single bucket
Headers: `x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256` (SSE-S3) or `aws:kms` (+ `-aws-kms-key-id`) for SSE-KMS; SSE-C uses `-customer-algorithm`, `-customer-key`, `-customer-key-MD5` on every request
Block Public Access (on by default), bucket policy, IAM
Object Ownership: ACLs disabled by default (bucket owner enforced)
aws:SecureTransport to enforce HTTPS; MFA Delete
Object Lock (requires versioning): Compliance = nobody, not even root, can delete/shorten retention; Governance = users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention can; legal hold = no expiry
Access Points to simplify access to shared buckets

Encrypting data stored in S3 (e.g. HIPAA): server-side encryption with AES-256 (SSE-S3, or SSE-KMS/SSE-C) and/or client-side encryption with your own keys before sending it over HTTPS; S3 has no AES-128 option, and encrypting EBS volumes or EBS snapshots does not encrypt objects stored in S3

Audit trail of who used the encryption key + envelope encryption + automatic rotation = SSE-KMS (key use is logged in CloudTrail); SSE-S3 has no per-use key audit and SSE-C means you supply and manage keys yourself
use_when: Key auditing and control over encryption access → SSE-KMS
Data must not be deletable for N years (WORM) → Object Lock Compliance
Bucket access only via CloudFront → OAC
not_for: SSE-KMS at high rps hits KMS quotas — use S3 Bucket Keys
"Strict regulatory" immutability with governance mode — it can be bypassed; use compliance mode
Headers containing `-customer-` are SSE-C only — never the answer for SSE-S3/SSE-KMS
AES-128 is never the S3 SSE answer — SSE uses AES-256

vs.note: SSE-KMS uses KMS keys and logs to CloudTrail
Macie finds PII and public buckets

services.name: S3 Performance (Transfer Acceleration, Multipart, Presigned URLs)
services.tagline: S3 performance: prefixes, multipart, acceleration
facts: 3500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5500 GET/HEAD rps per prefix
More prefixes → more parallel throughput
Multipart upload and byte-range fetches for parallelism
Transfer Acceleration for long-distance uploads
S3 Select / Express One Zone for low latency
use_when: Uploading large files from far away is slow → Transfer Acceleration + multipart
High request rate → spread across prefixes
not_for: Transfer Acceleration has no caching — for repeated downloads of the same files by many clients use CloudFront; TA shines for long-distance uploads

vs.note: CloudFront speeds up reads/delivery; Transfer Acceleration — uploads to S3

services.name: Amazon S3 Glacier
services.tagline: S3 Glacier archival classes: cheap, retrieval from ms to hours
facts: Instant Retrieval — ms; Flexible — Expedited 1–5 min, Standard 3–5 h, Bulk 5–12 h
Deep Archive — Standard up to 12 h, Bulk up to 48 h
Minimum storage duration 90 / 90 / 180 days
Vault Lock — WORM policy for a vault

Guaranteed fast retrieval (audit, "under all circumstances"): Expedited (1–5 min) + provisioned capacity units (each gives up to 150 MB/s and guarantees expedited requests succeed); Standard/Bulk too slow; range retrieval only reduces volume

Rare access with up to 24 h retrieval (audit data): S3 lifecycle rule transitioning to Glacier after 0 days archives immediately; Standard-IA/One Zone-IA cost more, One Zone-IA is also single-AZ, FSx is far costlier
use_when: Long-term storage for compliance
Replacement for tape archives
not_for: Data needed immediately (except Instant Retrieval) — a trap

vs.note: Glacier is part of the S3 classes
Tape Gateway writes virtual tapes to Glacier

services.name: Amazon EBS
services.tagline: Network block volumes for EC2 within one AZ
facts: Bound to an AZ; move via snapshot
gp3: 3000 IOPS and 125 MB/s baseline, independently configurable IOPS/throughput
io2 Block Express: up to 256000 IOPS, Multi-Attach (io1/io2)
st1 (throughput HDD), sc1 (cold HDD) — can't be boot volumes
Incremental snapshots in S3; cross-Region copy; Fast Snapshot Restore

Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1/io2) = consistent low latency for I/O-intensive databases (large relational/NoSQL); gp2/gp3 = general purpose (boot, dev/test, small-medium DBs); Magnetic (standard) = previous-generation HDD, lowest cost per GB, infrequent access. NOT EBS types: Spot volumes (Spot is an EC2 purchase model) and SR-IOV (an enhanced-networking technology); gp3 has no Multi-Attach and no multi-AZ

Encrypted EBS volume behavior: snapshots of an encrypted volume are automatically encrypted, volumes created from an encrypted snapshot are automatically encrypted, and all data moving between the volume and the instance is encrypted too (not just the data at rest on the volume)

Encryption at rest = KMS keys: the AWS managed key (aws/ebs) or your own customer managed key (symmetric only); covers data volumes, boot volumes and snapshots, AES-256, done on the host so data in transit between instance and volume is encrypted too. NOT S3 SSE/client-side encryption, NOT a password in CloudHSM, NOT ACM certificates

Facts for "is EBS suitable" questions: persists independently of the instance (off-instance storage); Elastic Volumes let you change type, size and IOPS live in production without interruption; replicated automatically only within its own AZ (not another Region) and attachable only to instances in the same AZ; snapshots go to S3, not RDS
Encryption via KMS; Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) — free, tag-based schedule for automated snapshot/AMI creation, retention and deletion
use_when: Boot/data volume for EC2, databases on EC2
High IOPS with low latency → io2
High sequential throughput cheaply → st1
"Automate EBS snapshots quickly, cheaply, simply" → Data Lifecycle Manager
not_for: Can't attach to an instance in another AZ
Shared FS for many instances → EFS

vs.note: Instance store is faster, but ephemeral
EFS — shared across many instances and AZs
FSx — managed Windows/Lustre/ONTAP/OpenZFS file systems

services.name: EC2 Instance Store
services.tagline: Local NVMe disk on the EC2 host: very fast, ephemeral
facts: Data is lost on stop, terminate, hibernate or host failure (reboot preserves it)
Stop/start: instance-store data lost + host may change, but Elastic IP and primary ENI stay attached
Very high IOPS / low latency
Size is fixed by the instance type
use_when: Buffer, cache, scratch data
Replicated data (Cassandra) with maximum IOPS
not_for: Persistent data — a trap, use EBS

vs.note: EBS — persistent network volume; instance store — ephemeral local disk

services.name: Amazon EFS
services.tagline: Managed NFS file system, shared across many Linux instances
facts: NFSv4, Linux only (POSIX)
Regional (Multi-AZ); One Zone option is cheaper
Grows automatically, pay per use
Storage classes: Standard, IA, Archive + lifecycle management
Throughput modes: Elastic (recommended), Provisioned, Bursting

Shared storage for hundreds of ECS tasks with constant high-frequency reads/writes (small data set, ~10 TB): EFS with Provisioned Throughput + Max I/O performance mode, mounted in the ECS task definition. Bursting throughput scales with stored size and cannot sustain constant heavy demand; performance mode is chosen at creation and cannot be changed. FSx for Windows is SMB for Windows workloads; DynamoDB is a database and cannot be mounted
Mounts in EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda
use_when: Shared file system for many Linux EC2 instances across AZs
Shared storage for containers/Lambda
Content management, web serving with shared files
not_for: Windows / SMB → FSx for Windows
HPC with ultra-high throughput → FSx for Lustre

vs.note: EBS — one instance, one AZ; EFS — many instances, many AZs
FSx — Windows SMB, Lustre HPC, ONTAP, OpenZFS
S3 — objects via API, cheaper; EFS — POSIX files

services.name: Amazon FSx (Windows / Lustre / NetApp ONTAP / OpenZFS)
services.tagline: Managed file systems: Windows, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS
facts: FSx for Windows File Server — SMB, NTFS, AD integration, DFS, Multi-AZ
FSx for Lustre — HPC/ML, hundreds of GB/s, S3 integration (lazy load, write back)
Lustre: scratch (temporary, cheap) vs persistent
FSx for NetApp ONTAP — NFS/SMB/iSCSI, NetApp migration
FSx for OpenZFS — NFS, ZFS migration
use_when: Windows apps with SMB and Active Directory → FSx for Windows
HPC/ML with data in S3 → FSx for Lustre
Lift-and-shift NetApp → FSx for ONTAP
not_for: Simple shared Linux NFS → EFS is simpler

vs.note: EFS — simple Linux NFS; FSx — specialized file systems
EBS — block disk for a single instance
FSx File Gateway provides an on-prem cache for FSx for Windows

services.name: AWS Storage Gateway
services.tagline: Hybrid: on-prem access to cloud storage via a local cache
facts: S3 File Gateway — NFS/SMB → S3 objects (each file = one S3 object, local cache); on-prem backups over file protocols → File Gateway, not DataSync/EBS
FSx File Gateway — local cache for FSx for Windows
Volume Gateway — iSCSI: cached (data in S3) or stored (data local, backups in S3); data lives as EBS snapshots, NOT readable via S3 API
Tape Gateway — virtual tape library (VTL) → S3/Glacier
Deployed as a VM or hardware appliance
use_when: On-prem apps need to access S3 as a file share
Replace physical backup tapes → Tape Gateway
Extend local storage into the cloud with low latency for frequently accessed data
not_for: One-time migration of a large volume → DataSync/Snowball
Not for backing up EBS volumes (use DLM / AWS Backup)
Moving data out once to free on-prem space — that's migration (DataSync), Storage Gateway keeps on-prem apps using cloud storage

vs.note: DataSync — data transfer/sync; Storage Gateway — ongoing hybrid access
FSx File Gateway caches FSx for Windows on-prem

services.name: AWS Backup
services.tagline: Centralized backup policies for many services
facts: Supports EC2, EBS, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, S3, Storage Gateway, etc.
Backup plans: schedule, retention, lifecycle to cold storage — the way to keep RDS/Aurora backups longer than the 35-day automated limit (e.g. 90 days)
Cross-Region and cross-account copies
Backup Vault Lock — WORM, protection against deletion
Integration with Organizations (backup policies)
use_when: Unified backups for many services with LEAST operational overhead
Compliance: undeletable backups
Backup copies to another Region/account for DR
"Automated cross-account backup of DynamoDB for long-term retention" → AWS Backup plan with cross-account copy
not_for: Not for continuous replication (that's S3 replication / DRS)

vs.note: Replication — live copy; Backup — scheduled recovery points
DRS — continuous server replication with low RPO
EBS-only snapshot automation → DLM (simplest); many services/accounts, vault lock → AWS Backup

categories.name: Databases
categories.summary: Relational (RDS, Aurora), NoSQL (DynamoDB), in-memory and purpose-built databases, and their HA/scaling.

services.name: Amazon RDS
services.tagline: Managed relational DBs: MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2
facts: AWS handles patching, backups, failover; no OS access (except RDS Custom)
Automated backups: retention up to 35 days, point-in-time restore
Manual snapshots are kept indefinitely; cross-Region copy
Storage autoscaling; encryption only at creation (otherwise snapshot → copy encrypted → restore)
IAM database authentication (MySQL/PostgreSQL only, not SQL Server)

Encrypt in-flight data to RDS (e.g. SQL Server): download the RDS root CA certificate, import it on the clients and configure the application to connect with SSL, and force SSL for every connection with the rds.force_ssl parameter = true (static parameter: reboot the DB instance). TDE only encrypts data at rest on SQL Server/Oracle, IAM DB authentication is only a login method, and security groups on port 443 do not encrypt anything (databases do not listen on 443)
use_when: Relational OLTP workload without managing the DB
Need SQL, joins, transactions
not_for: Need OS access / customization → RDS Custom or EC2
Unlimited key-value scaling → DynamoDB

vs.note: Aurora is faster, 6 copies across 3 AZs, up to 15 replicas, fast failover
DynamoDB — serverless NoSQL, single-digit ms at any scale

services.name: RDS Multi-AZ
services.tagline: Synchronous standby in another AZ for HA and automatic failover
facts: Synchronous replication; automatic failover (~1–2 min) by flipping the endpoint's DNS CNAME to the standby — same endpoint name, app just reconnects
Failover triggers — PRIMARY only: AZ outage, network loss, compute or storage failure, OS patching / instance class change, reboot with failover
The standby (Multi-AZ instance) doesn't serve reads
Multi-AZ DB cluster: 2 readable standbys, failover ~35 s
Backups are taken from the standby — no load on the primary
use_when: High availability and automatic DB failover
Survive an AZ failure
not_for: Doesn't scale reads (instance deployment) → Read Replicas
Not cross-Region DR
Standby (secondary) or Read Replica failures don't trigger failover — RDS just replaces the standby
Failover doesn't move the IP or spin up a new instance to serve traffic — it's a CNAME flip to the existing standby

vs.note: Read replicas — asynchronous, for read scaling; Multi-AZ — for HA
In Aurora, HA is achieved via replicas in other AZs

services.name: RDS Read Replicas
services.tagline: Asynchronous copies for read scaling
facts: Up to 15 read replicas (RDS MySQL/MariaDB/PostgreSQL; Aurora — 15)
Asynchronous → eventual consistency, replica lag
Can be in the same AZ, another AZ or another Region (cross-Region)
Can be promoted to a standalone DB (DR)
The application must use a separate endpoint for reads
use_when: Heavy reads/reports load the primary
Analytics queries must not affect production
Cross-Region DR with the ability to promote
not_for: Doesn't provide automatic failover like Multi-AZ (for RDS)

vs.note: Multi-AZ — synchronous HA; Read Replicas — asynchronous read scaling
ElastiCache reduces load via caching, with lower latency

services.name: Amazon RDS Proxy
services.tagline: Managed connection pool for RDS/Aurora
facts: Connection pooling — critical for Lambda (many short-lived connections)
Reduces failover time by up to ~66%
IAM authentication, secrets in Secrets Manager
Serverless, Multi-AZ, accessible only from within the VPC
use_when: Lambda exhausts connections to RDS
Speed up failover and improve application resilience
not_for: Doesn't cache query data (that's ElastiCache)

vs.note: ElastiCache caches results; RDS Proxy pools connections
Typical pair: Lambda + RDS Proxy

services.name: Amazon Aurora
services.tagline: Cloud relational DB compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL
facts: 6 copies of data across 3 AZs; storage grows automatically up to 256 TiB
Up to 15 Aurora Replicas, failover usually < 30 s
Writer endpoint, reader endpoint (load-balanced), custom endpoints
Backtrack (MySQL), cloning, Aurora Auto Scaling replicas
Aurora I/O-Optimized for I/O-intensive workloads
use_when: High-performance, highly available relational DB
Read-heavy with replica autoscaling
Fast clone of production for testing
not_for: Need Oracle/SQL Server → RDS

vs.note: RDS — more engines; Aurora — higher performance and HA
Serverless v2 — ACU autoscaling for variable load
DynamoDB — NoSQL key-value

services.name: Aurora Serverless
services.tagline: Aurora with automatic capacity scaling (ACU)
facts: Serverless v2 scales instantly in 0.5 ACU increments
Can scale down to 0 ACU (auto-pause) in current versions
Supports Multi-AZ, read replicas, Global Database
Billed per ACU-second
Provisioned → Serverless v2 with minimal downtime: add a Serverless v2 reader to the cluster, then fail over (no snapshot/DMS)
use_when: Unpredictable/variable or infrequent workload
Dev/test DB that is often idle
not_for: Steady constant load — provisioned may be cheaper

vs.note: Provisioned Aurora — fixed instance size
DynamoDB on-demand — the serverless NoSQL counterpart

services.name: Aurora Global Database
services.tagline: Aurora Global Database: replication to other Regions with < 1 s lag
facts: 1 primary Region + up to 10 secondary Regions (read-only)
Storage-level replication, usually < 1 s
Managed failover/switchover; RTO about 1 minute, RPO ~ seconds
Write forwarding from secondary Regions
use_when: Global application with low read latency worldwide
Cross-Region DR with RPO of seconds and RTO ~1 min
not_for: For HA within a Region, replicas in multiple AZs are enough

vs.note: RDS cross-Region read replica is slower with higher lag
DynamoDB Global Tables — multi-active writes in all Regions

services.name: Amazon DynamoDB
services.tagline: Serverless NoSQL key-value/document DB with single-digit ms latency
facts: Item up to 400 KB; partition key (+ sort key)
On-demand or provisioned capacity (with auto scaling)
Auto Scaling is on by default only when the table is created in the console — tables created via CLI/API/IaC have NONE until you enable it
GSI (different PK, eventual consistency) and LSI (only at table creation)

Streams (24 h, ordered item-level changes) → Lambda event source mapping: the way to react to new items with no change to the writer app (not SNS from the producer, CloudWatch alarms or Systems Manager); TTL for automatic deletion

PITR up to 35 days (restore to a NEW table, same Region and same account); on-demand backups; export to S3; automated cross-account / long-term retention copies → AWS Backup (copy the backup to a vault in another account); the native on-demand backups and PITR do not copy cross-account, and Timestream is not a recovery tool
Transactions; strongly consistent reads optional
use_when: Stem says "key-value", "document model" or "provisioned/on-demand capacity mode" → DynamoDB (capacity modes are DynamoDB terminology)
Scalable key-value DB with LEAST operational overhead
Sessions, shopping carts, gaming leaderboards, IoT
Unpredictable traffic → on-demand
Embedded/self-managed NoSQL DB overloads the web tier → migrate to DynamoDB (DMS ongoing replication): multi-AZ, eventually consistent by default
not_for: Complex joins/ad-hoc SQL → RDS/Aurora
Items > 400 KB — store in S3, keep a reference in DynamoDB
Don't confuse with WorkDocs — end-user file collaboration, not a database
PITR is not cross-account or long-term retention — use AWS Backup copy

vs.note: RDS — SQL and joins; DynamoDB — NoSQL, horizontal scaling
DAX — in-memory cache with microsecond latency for DynamoDB
DocumentDB — MongoDB-compatible document DB

services.name: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
services.tagline: In-memory cache for DynamoDB with microsecond latency
facts: API-compatible with DynamoDB — minimal code changes
Caches items and query results
Microsecond reads for hot items; pair with DynamoDB Auto Scaling (DAX doesn't scale table capacity)
Cluster in a VPC, Multi-AZ
use_when: Read-heavy DynamoDB, need microsecond latency
Hot keys
not_for: Doesn't cache other DBs (for RDS — ElastiCache)
Doesn't help write-heavy workloads

vs.note: ElastiCache — general-purpose cache; DAX — transparent, DynamoDB only
DAX sits in front of DynamoDB

services.name: DynamoDB Global Tables & Streams
services.tagline: DynamoDB Global Tables: multi-Region, multi-active replication
facts: Writes and reads in any Region (active-active)
Asynchronous replication usually < 1 s (multi-Region strong consistency option available)
Last writer wins on conflicts
Requires DynamoDB Streams
use_when: Global application with local writes in multiple Regions
Multi-Region DR with RPO ≈ 0

vs.note: Aurora Global — one writer Region; Global Tables — writes everywhere

services.name: Amazon ElastiCache (Redis / Memcached)
services.tagline: Managed in-memory cache: Valkey, Redis OSS, Memcached
facts: Valkey/Redis OSS: replication, Multi-AZ failover, persistence, pub/sub, sorted sets
Memcached: simple multithreaded cache, no replication/persistence
Patterns: lazy loading (cache-aside), write-through, TTL
Session store for stateless applications
Requires application code changes; serverless option available
use_when: Reduce load on RDS and read latency
Store user sessions outside the instances
Leaderboard (sorted sets)
not_for: Cache for DynamoDB without code changes → DAX
Durable storage of the primary copy of data → MemoryDB

vs.note: DAX — DynamoDB only, transparent
MemoryDB — durable primary DB; ElastiCache — cache
Replicas scale DB reads; a cache gives lower latency

services.name: Amazon DocumentDB
services.tagline: Managed document DB compatible with MongoDB
facts: Storage architecture like Aurora (6 copies, 3 AZs)
Up to 15 replicas; storage grows automatically
Elastic clusters for sharding
use_when: Migrating MongoDB workloads to a managed service
JSON documents with a flexible schema

vs.note: DynamoDB — key-value AWS-native; DocumentDB — MongoDB API

services.name: Amazon Neptune
services.tagline: Managed graph DB
facts: Gremlin, openCypher, SPARQL
Up to 15 read replicas, Multi-AZ
Neptune Analytics for graph analytics
use_when: Social networks, recommendations, fraud detection, knowledge graphs
Highly connected data
