services.name: Amazon Keyspaces
services.tagline: Serverless managed DB compatible with Apache Cassandra
facts: CQL API; serverless, on-demand or provisioned
Replication across 3 AZs; multi-Region replication
Point-in-time recovery, encryption at rest by default
use_when: Migrating Cassandra without managing a cluster
Need the CQL API without managing nodes and patching

vs.note: DynamoDB — native AWS NoSQL; Keyspaces — Cassandra API

services.name: Amazon Timestream
services.tagline: Serverless time-series DB
facts: For IoT, metrics, telemetry
Timestream for LiveAnalytics (memory and magnetic tiers) and Timestream for InfluxDB
Built-in time-series functions
use_when: IoT telemetry, application metrics, timestamped data
Keep recent data in memory, older data cheaply, automatically

vs.note: DynamoDB works, but Timestream is optimized for time series

services.name: Amazon QLDB
services.tagline: Ledger DB with an immutable, verifiable journal (service discontinued)
facts: Immutable journal, SHA-256 verification of history
End of support 07/31/2025 — AWS recommends Aurora PostgreSQL
May appear in older questions
use_when: Older questions: immutable change history, transaction auditing
Older questions: central trusted journal (system of record)
not_for: Don't choose it for new solutions (service discontinued)

vs.note: AWS recommends migrating QLDB to Aurora PostgreSQL

services.name: Amazon MemoryDB
services.tagline: Durable in-memory DB compatible with Valkey/Redis OSS
facts: Multi-AZ transaction log — no data loss
Microsecond reads, single-digit ms writes
Can be the primary DB, not just a cache
use_when: Need Redis speed with primary-DB durability
Redis-compatible store where data loss is unacceptable
not_for: If you only need a cache — ElastiCache is cheaper

vs.note: ElastiCache — cache; MemoryDB — durable primary database

categories.name: Application Integration
categories.summary: Asynchronous decoupling of components: queues, pub/sub, event buses, brokers, and SaaS/email integration.

services.name: Amazon SQS
services.tagline: Managed message queue for decoupling (pull model)
facts: Standard: nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once, ordering not guaranteed
Message size: classically 256 KB (as on the exam), since 2025 up to 1 MiB; larger → Extended Client + S3
Retention 1 min – 14 days (default 4 days)
Visibility timeout default 30 s, max 12 h
ASG can scale on ApproximateNumberOfMessages (backlog per instance)
DLQ after maxReceiveCount; delay queues up to 15 min; long polling up to 20 s
use_when: Decouple producer and consumer, buffer during load spikes
Don't lose orders when workers fail
Scale workers by queue depth
Decouple components running both on EC2 and on-premises (public HTTPS API)
not_for: Need to broadcast to many subscribers → SNS (or SNS + SQS fan-out)
Strict ordering → FIFO
SQS can't filter messages server-side — filter upstream with SNS filter policies or EventBridge rules

vs.note: SNS — push pub/sub to many; SQS — pull queue for one type of consumer
EventBridge — rule-based event routing, SaaS sources
Kinesis — stream with replay and multiple consumers, ordering per shard

services.name: SQS FIFO
services.tagline: SQS FIFO: strict ordering and exactly-once processing
facts: Queue name must end with .fifo
300 msg/s without batching, 3,000 with batching; high throughput mode — much more
Message group ID — ordering within a group; deduplication ID / content-based dedup (5-min window)
Exactly-once processing
use_when: Order of operations is critical (transactions, commands)
Duplicates must not be processed
not_for: Need massive throughput with no ordering requirement → Standard

vs.note: Standard — higher throughput, at-least-once, no ordering
SNS FIFO topic + SQS FIFO — ordered fan-out

services.name: Amazon SNS
services.tagline: Pub/sub: push messages to many subscribers
facts: Subscribers: SQS, Lambda, HTTP/S, email, SMS, mobile push, Firehose
Fan-out: SNS → multiple SQS queues
Subscription filter policies (JSON on message attributes or body): each subscriber gets only matching messages — no routing code
Messages up to 256 KB; FIFO topics for ordering
No message storage — undelivered messages are lost without a DLQ
use_when: One event → multiple independent handlers (fan-out)
Email/SMS notifications
CloudWatch Alarm alerts
"Separate queue per message type / message filtering" → one topic + SQS subscriptions with filter policies
Alert a team by SMS/email when an event is detected (e.g. Rekognition finding)
not_for: Need buffering and reprocessing → add SQS

EventBridge — advanced filtering/routing, schemas, SaaS, archive/replay

services.name: Amazon EventBridge
services.tagline: Serverless event bus: routing rules for events from AWS, SaaS, and your own apps
facts: Default bus (AWS events), custom buses, partner (SaaS) buses
Rules with event patterns → targets (Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, etc.)
Scheduler — cron/rate schedules (replaces CloudWatch Events)
Event archive and replay; Schema Registry
Pipes: source → filter/enrich → target; cross-account/cross-region buses
use_when: React to AWS service events (EC2 state change, GuardDuty finding)
Integrate SaaS events (Zendesk, Datadog)
Run Lambda on a schedule
Event-driven architecture with content-based filtering
not_for: Not a pull queue with long retention → SQS

vs.note: SNS — simple high-throughput fan-out; EventBridge — rich filtering and SaaS
SQS — queue; EventBridge — event router

services.name: Amazon MQ
services.tagline: Managed Apache ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ broker
facts: Protocols: AMQP, MQTT, OpenWire, STOMP, JMS
Active/standby across two AZs for HA
Runs on instances — scales worse than SQS/SNS
use_when: Migrate on-prem apps using ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ without rewriting code
Need standard protocols (AMQP, MQTT, JMS)
not_for: New cloud-native application → SQS/SNS

services.name: Amazon AppFlow
services.tagline: Managed data transfer between SaaS (Salesforce, SAP, Slack) and AWS
facts: Sources: Salesforce, SAP, Zendesk, Slack, ServiceNow, etc.
Destinations: S3, Redshift, Snowflake, etc.
On a schedule, on an event, or on demand; filtering, mapping
Can run over PrivateLink

Bidirectional SaaS ↔ AWS data exchange on a schedule/event

services.name: Amazon SES
services.tagline: Send and receive email (transactional and marketing)
facts: SMTP interface and API
DKIM, SPF, DMARC; reputation and delivery metrics
Inbound email → S3, Lambda, SNS

services.name: Amazon SWF (Simple Workflow Service)
services.tagline: Legacy workflow coordination with workers that can run anywhere

Workflow executions up to 1 year; tasks assigned exactly once, tracked state

categories.name: Analytics & Streaming
categories.summary: Stream processing, ETL, data lakes, data warehouses, search, and BI visualization.

services.name: Kinesis Data Streams
services.tagline: Real-time data stream with shards, replay, and multiple consumers
facts: Retention 24 h by default, up to 365 days
Provisioned (per shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s write, 2 MB/s read) or on-demand
Ordering guaranteed within a shard (partition key)
Enhanced fan-out — 2 MB/s per consumer per shard

Clickstream / user-activity analytics: Kinesis ingests real-time events (with Lambda@Edge/CloudFront for global proximity) and results land durably in S3; Athena queries S3 but does not process streams
Records up to 1 MB (current limit up to 10 MB); consumers: Lambda, KCL, Flink, Firehose
use_when: Real-time processing of clickstream, logs, IoT with multiple consumers
Need data replay
Per-key ordering at high throughput
Custom async processing of stream records → Lambda consumer (event source mapping), cheapest if each batch finishes in < 15 min
not_for: Just deliver data to S3/Redshift with no code → Firehose
Simple task decoupling → SQS

services.name: Amazon Data Firehose (Kinesis Data Firehose)
services.tagline: Amazon Data Firehose: managed stream delivery to S3/Redshift/OpenSearch/Splunk
facts: Formerly Kinesis Data Firehose
Fully serverless, auto scaling, no shards
Near real-time: buffering by size/time (0 s to 900 s)
Transformation via Lambda, conversion to Parquet/ORC, compression
Destinations: S3, Redshift (via S3), OpenSearch, Splunk, HTTP endpoints, Apache Iceberg tables
No replay/data retention

Convert JSON to Parquet on the fly
not_for: Need millisecond real-time and custom consumers / replay → Kinesis Data Streams

services.name: Amazon Kinesis Video Streams

use_when: Real-time aggregations/windows over a stream (anomalies, metrics)
Streaming ETL on Apache Flink
not_for: Simple delivery to S3 without analytics → Firehose

Multi-AZ brokers

not_for: If Kafka isn't required, AWS-native KDS is simpler

services.name: Amazon Athena
services.tagline: Serverless SQL queries directly against data in S3
facts: Pay per data scanned (~$5 per TB)
Optimization: Parquet/ORC, compression, partitioning → less data scanned
Uses the Glue Data Catalog
Federated queries to other sources via Lambda connectors
use_when: Ad-hoc SQL analysis of logs in S3 (CloudTrail, ALB, VPC Flow Logs)
One-off queries with no data loading or infrastructure
not_for: Frequent, complex, high-performance BI queries → Redshift

Data integration with LEAST operational overhead

Built on the Glue Data Catalog
Blueprints for data ingestion; LF-Tags
Cross-account data sharing

Column/row-level access control for Athena/Redshift/EMR

categories.name: Migration & Transfer

services.name: AWS DMS
services.tagline: Database Migration Service: database migration and replication with minimal downtime
facts: Source stays available during migration
Homogeneous (Oracle→Oracle) and heterogeneous (Oracle→Aurora, requires schema conversion)

Replication instance or DMS Serverless; Multi-AZ

use_when: Migrate a database to AWS with minimal downtime
Continuous replication of an on-prem database to AWS (CDC)

Migrate a self-managed/embedded NoSQL DB (e.g. MongoDB) into DynamoDB with ongoing replication

services.name: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT)
services.tagline: Schema Conversion Tool: convert database schema and code between engines

Required for heterogeneous migration (Oracle → PostgreSQL)

Not needed for same-engine migrations

Assess conversion complexity

Destinations: S3 (writes directly into any storage class, incl. Glacier Deep Archive), EFS, FSx
Agent on-prem; no agent needed between AWS services
Encryption, integrity verification, preserves metadata/permissions
Scheduling, bandwidth throttling

Recurring on-prem → AWS sync
Copy between EFS/FSx/S3

not_for: Very large volume over a slow link → Snowball

Authentication: service-managed, AD, custom IdP (Lambda)
Existing clients stay unchanged

Works without network connectivity (edge)

Strategy recommendations; Migration Evaluator for TCO

Failback after recovery

Speaker diarization, custom vocabulary, PII redaction
Call Analytics: transcript + sentiment, talk time, issue detection for contact centers
Fully managed — no ML model to build or maintain
use_when: Turn call recordings/audio into text
Feed transcripts to Translate/Comprehend for analysis
not_for: Text-to-speech → Polly
Translating text → Translate
Sentiment/entities of text → Comprehend

vs.note: Transcribe — speech to text; Polly — text to speech
Lex — conversational chatbot (ASR+NLU); Transcribe — plain transcription

services.name: Amazon Translate
services.tagline: Neural machine translation of text between languages
facts: Real-time and batch translation, 75+ languages
Custom terminology and formality settings
Fully managed API — new languages need no model work
use_when: Translate transcripts/text (e.g. Hindi → English)
Localize content at scale
not_for: Audio to text → Transcribe
Sentiment analysis → Comprehend

vs.note: Translate — changes language; Comprehend — analyzes text (sentiment, entities)

services.name: Amazon Comprehend
services.tagline: NLP: sentiment, entities, key phrases, language detection, PII
facts: Sentiment analysis: positive, negative, neutral, mixed
Entity, key phrase, language and PII detection; topic modeling
Custom classification/entity models via managed training (optional)
Fully managed — no ML model to maintain for standard analysis
use_when: Sentiment of customer feedback, reviews or call transcripts
Extract entities/PII from text
not_for: Audio input directly → Transcribe first
Image/video analysis → Rekognition
Enterprise document search → Kendra

vs.note: Comprehend — understand text; Translate — convert between languages
Kendra — search over documents; Comprehend — analyze text content

services.name: Amazon Polly
services.tagline: Text-to-speech: lifelike voices from text
facts: Neural and standard voices, many languages
SSML for pronunciation/pauses; speech marks
Async synthesis to S3 (StartSpeechSynthesisTask)
use_when: Turn text into spoken audio (IVR, accessibility, apps)
not_for: Speech to text → Transcribe
Translation → Translate

vs.note: Polly — text to speech; Transcribe — speech to text

services.name: Amazon Lex
services.tagline: Build conversational chatbots/voicebots (ASR + NLU)
facts: Same technology as Alexa; intents, slots, utterances
Integrates with Amazon Connect, Lambda fulfillment, Slack/Facebook channels
Not a transcription service for recordings
use_when: Chatbot or IVR voicebot with natural-language intents
not_for: Transcribing call recordings → Transcribe
Sentiment analysis → Comprehend

vs.note: Lex — dialog/intent bot; Transcribe — speech to text only

services.name: Amazon Textract
services.tagline: Extract text, forms and tables from scanned documents
facts: OCR plus forms (key-value pairs) and tables extraction
Queries, signatures, ID and invoice analysis
Fully managed; results to S3/Lambda
use_when: Digitize scanned PDFs, invoices, forms
not_for: Images of objects/faces → Rekognition
Search over documents → Kendra

vs.note: Textract — structured document text; Rekognition — objects/faces, text in scenes

services.name: Amazon Rekognition
services.tagline: Image and video analysis: faces, people, objects, text, moderation
facts: Face detection, comparison and search against a face collection (e.g. authorized staff)
Rekognition Video analyzes Kinesis Video Streams in real time
Results → SNS/Lambda for alerts
Content moderation, PPE detection, celebrity recognition
use_when: Detect people/faces in camera feeds, unauthorized personnel
Moderate user-uploaded images/videos
not_for: Text search over documents → Kendra
Fraud scoring → Fraud Detector

vs.note: Rekognition — ready-made vision API; SageMaker — build/train your own model

services.name: Amazon Kendra
services.tagline: ML-powered enterprise search over documents
facts: Natural-language search across S3, SharePoint, Confluence, etc.
Connectors + relevance tuning
use_when: Intelligent search over internal documents
not_for: Image/video analysis → Rekognition

vs.note: OpenSearch — self-tuned search/log analytics; Kendra — managed semantic document search

services.name: Amazon SageMaker
services.tagline: Build, train and deploy custom ML models
facts: Notebooks, training jobs, endpoints; Autopilot = AutoML on tabular data
Use when no managed AI service fits
use_when: Custom model on your own data
not_for: Standard vision/text tasks with LEAST overhead → managed AI services (Rekognition, Comprehend…)

vs.note: Managed API vs building your own model

services.name: Amazon Fraud Detector
services.tagline: Managed fraud scoring for online events (payments, sign-ups)
facts: Detects fake accounts, payment fraud from event data
use_when: Online transaction / account-signup fraud
not_for: Video or image analysis → Rekognition

categories.name: Architecture Concepts
categories.summary: Cross-cutting exam architecture principles: HA, DR, scaling, decoupling, caching, encryption, and shared responsibility.

services.name: Regions, AZs, Edge Locations
services.tagline: Regions, Availability Zones, Local Zones, edge locations
facts: Region = multiple (usually 3+) isolated AZs
AZ = one or more data centers with independent power, connected by a low-latency network
Local Zones and Wavelength — compute closer to users/5G
Edge locations — CloudFront, Route 53, Global Accelerator
Region selection: compliance/data residency, latency, service availability, price
use_when: Requirement: data must not leave the country → choose the Region
HA → spread across multiple AZs
not_for: A single AZ ≠ high availability

vs.note: Multi-AZ — HA; multi-region — DR and global latency
Edge locations are used by CloudFront

services.name: AWS Well-Architected Framework
services.tagline: Well-Architected Framework: 6 pillars of best practices
facts: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability
Well-Architected Tool — workload reviews in the console
Lenses for specific domains (serverless, SaaS, etc.)
use_when: Questions about principles: automation, least privilege, scaling, managed services
Review a workload's architecture against best practices

vs.note: Trusted Advisor — automated checks; W-A — review methodology

services.name: High Availability & Fault Tolerance
services.tagline: High availability: survive component and AZ failures without downtime
facts: Multi-AZ everywhere: ELB + ASG in ≥2 AZs, RDS Multi-AZ, one NAT Gateway per AZ
Eliminate single points of failure
Managed regional services (S3, DynamoDB, SQS, Lambda) are already Multi-AZ
Health checks + automatic replacement
use_when: Application must stay available if an AZ fails
Minimize downtime
not_for: HA ≠ DR: HA is within a Region, DR is recovery from a major disaster
Scaling ≠ HA

vs.note: DR — survive a Region failure; HA — survive an AZ/component failure
RDS Multi-AZ — the classic HA example for databases

services.name: DR Strategies (Backup & Restore / Pilot Light / Warm Standby / Multi-Site)
services.tagline: DR strategies: Backup & Restore → Pilot Light → Warm Standby → Multi-site
facts: Backup & Restore — cheapest, RPO/RTO in hours
Pilot Light — core (database) replicated, the rest launched during a disaster; RTO tens of minutes
Warm Standby — scaled-down fully functional copy, scaled up on failover; RTO minutes
Multi-site active/active — near-zero RTO/RPO, most expensive
Tools: AWS Backup, DRS, Aurora Global, DynamoDB Global Tables, Route 53 failover
use_when: Cheapest DR when hours of downtime are acceptable → Backup & Restore
Minimal cost but RTO of minutes to tens of minutes → Pilot Light / Warm Standby
Zero downtime → Multi-site active/active
not_for: Pilot Light ≠ Warm Standby: in Pilot Light the app servers are off

vs.note: RTO/RPO requirements determine the strategy
DRS — service for server DR
HA — within a Region; DR — across Regions

services.name: RTO / RPO
services.tagline: RTO — how long you can be down; RPO — how much data you can lose
facts: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) — maximum time to recover
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) — maximum acceptable period of data loss
RPO is determined by backup/replication frequency
Lower RTO/RPO → more expensive solution
use_when: "No more than 5 minutes of data loss" → RPO 5 min (continuous replication)
"Recover within 1 hour" → RTO 1 h
not_for: Don't confuse them: RPO is about data, RTO is about time

vs.note: The DR strategy is chosen to meet RTO/RPO

services.name: Decoupling & Loose Coupling
services.tagline: Decoupling components via queues, events, and streams
facts: Asynchronous communication: SQS (queue), SNS (pub/sub), EventBridge (events), Kinesis (streams)
A buffer smooths spikes; producer and consumer scale independently
Fan-out: SNS → multiple SQS queues
Idempotent consumers due to at-least-once delivery
use_when: A component fails under peak load / loses requests
Loose coupling, microservices
Independent scaling of tiers
not_for: Synchronous calls between tiers — a common cause of data loss in exam questions
Databases (RDS, DynamoDB) or networking (VPC peering) are not decoupling services

vs.note: SQS — the primary decoupling tool
SNS — fan-out
EventBridge — event routing

services.name: Caching Strategies
services.tagline: Caching at every layer to lower latency and reduce load
facts: Edge: CloudFront; API: API Gateway cache
Application/database: ElastiCache, DAX for DynamoDB
Strategies: lazy loading (cache-aside), write-through, TTL
Cache invalidation vs stale data — a trade-off
use_when: Reduce database load from repeated reads
Lower latency for global users
not_for: Caching doesn't suit frequently changing data that requires strong consistency

vs.note: ElastiCache — cache for databases/sessions
CloudFront — edge cache
DAX — DynamoDB cache

services.name: Encryption at Rest / in Transit
services.tagline: Encryption at rest and in transit on AWS
facts: At rest: KMS (SSE-KMS, EBS, RDS), SSE-S3, CloudHSM
In transit: TLS/HTTPS (ACM), VPN IPsec, MACsec on DX
RDS: encryption can only be enabled at creation; unencrypted → snapshot → encrypted copy → restore
Client-side encryption — you encrypt before sending to AWS (with a KMS key or your own client-side master key); 'encrypt before upload' is never SSE
Encrypted snapshots can be shared only with a customer managed key
use_when: Requirement to encrypt data at rest and in transit
Key control → customer managed key / CloudHSM
"AWS must never see plaintext / keys stay with us" → client-side encryption before upload (+ HTTPS in transit)
not_for: Encrypting an existing RDS instance "in place" is not possible

vs.note: KMS — the foundation of encryption at rest
ACM — certificates for in-transit encryption

services.name: Shared Responsibility Model
services.tagline: Shared Responsibility Model: AWS — "of the cloud", customer — "in the cloud"
facts: AWS: physical security, hardware, network, hypervisor, managed services
Customer: data, IAM, SG/NACL configuration, encryption, OS and patches on EC2
For managed services (RDS, Lambda) AWS patches the OS/engine; the customer handles access, data, settings
Shared: patch management, configuration management, training
use_when: Who patches the OS on EC2 (customer) or RDS (AWS)
Who is responsible for data encryption, IAM, and SG settings (customer)

vs.note: IAM and access management are always the customer's responsibility

services.name: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
services.tagline: Vertical and horizontal scaling, elasticity
facts: Vertical (scale up) — bigger instance, has a ceiling and downtime
Horizontal (scale out) — more instances, requires statelessness
Stateless: sessions in ElastiCache/DynamoDB, files in S3/EFS
Read-heavy databases: read replicas + cache; write-heavy: sharding, DynamoDB
use_when: Load varies during the day → Auto Scaling (horizontal)
Make the application stateless so it can scale
"Single EC2, users will grow, add elasticity" → multiple instances behind ELB (+ ASG) or Route 53 weighted/multivalue across instances
not_for: Sticky sessions hinder even scaling

vs.note: ASG — horizontal scaling of EC2
Replicas — scaling database reads

services.name: Consistency Models
services.tagline: Data consistency models in AWS services
facts: S3 — strong read-after-write consistency for all operations
DynamoDB — eventual by default, strongly consistent reads optional (not for GSIs)
RDS read replicas — asynchronous (eventual), Multi-AZ — synchronous
Global replicas (Aurora Global, Global Tables) — asynchronous with lag
use_when: Need to read just-written data → strongly consistent read / primary endpoint
Choose a database based on read consistency requirements
not_for: Reading from a read replica right after a write may return stale data

vs.note: DynamoDB: choose between eventual and strong consistency
Replica lag — the source of eventual consistency

services.name: Partitioning & Sharding
services.tagline: Sharding and distributing load by key
facts: DynamoDB: high-cardinality partition key to avoid hot partitions
Kinesis: partition key → shard, ordering within a shard
S3: throughput is per prefix — spread across prefixes
SQS FIFO: message group ID for parallelism with ordering
use_when: Throttling due to a hot key
Scale writes horizontally
not_for: Low-cardinality key (date, status) — hot partition trap

vs.note: Partition key choice determines scalability
Shards and partition key define parallelism
